newsitem.title: USA: Judge throws out just one claim in USAir case.
newsitem.headline: Judge throws out just one claim in USAir case.

text.p: A federal judge Friday tossed out one of the issues in USAir's suit against British Airways Plc and AMR Corp., but left the remaining claims undecided for now.

U.S. District Court Judge Miriam Cedarbaum dismissed USAir's claim of tortious interference against AMR, the parent of American Airlines, but gave no indication when she would decide on the remaining claims.
British Airways said USAir's suit should be dismissed, calling it a tactic to renegotiate the 1993 deal between British Airways and USAir.

USAir's suit is "not a complaint on a legal matter, but an existential whine by USAir's current management that they don't like the agreement they made with British Airways," John Warden, a lawyer for British Airways said during the hearing Friday.
Three years ago, British Airways gained a 24.6 percent stake in USAir and three seats on the airline's board in exchange for a $300 million capital infusion.

USAir alleges in its suit that a proposed marketing alliance between American Airlines and British Airways, announced in June, undermines the existing pact between USAir and British Airways and monopolises air travel between the United States and Britain.
British Airways and American insist that their proposed alliance, which remains contigent on the formation of a new Anglo-American air treaty, would not inhibit competition.
USAir, however, contends it lost its "independent right to compete."
British Airways and American "conspired together to prevent USAir from engaging in other competitive opportunities," Shep Goldfein, a lawyer for USAir, said in the hearing Friday.
"They are foreclosing competition. There is injury to the travelling public and injury to USAir," Goldfein said.
USAir also called British Airway's presence on its board "a gorilla on our back."
With British Airways on its board, USAir contends it would not be able to compete fairly for new slots or routes that may open up at London Heathrow Airport if a new U.S.-U.K. air treaty was formed.
"Everyone knows we can't get slots, we can't get routes while we are still part of the British Airways family," Goldfein said.
On Thursday, USAir distanced itself further from its British partner, saying it will end itsBritish Airways code-sharing pact as of March 29.
